findings.title: New order() method is abstract and breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations
findings.body: CryptoProvider is an SPI loaded through ServiceLoader, but order() was added as an abstract method. Existing external or test implementations compiled against the previous interface do not implement it, so recompilation fails and already-compiled providers will throw AbstractMethodError when CryptoIntegration sorting invokes order(). This can prevent crypto-provider detection at startup. order() should be a default method, with only providers that need non-default precedence overriding it.

findings.title: Equal-priority crypto providers are silently selected in classpath-dependent order
findings.body: The change removes the previous fail-fast error for multiple CryptoProvider implementations and instead sorts by order() and silently uses the first provider, logging the others only at debug level. DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, and FIPS1402Provider all return order 200, so when more than one is present the winner depends on ServiceLoader/classpath iteration order. In particular, an environment accidentally containing both FIPS and non-FIPS providers could silently run with the non-FIPS provider instead of failing, creating a compliance and security risk. The providers need distinct priorities, especially for FIPS, or detection should fail/warn prominently on a tie for the highest priority.

findings.title: getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the default keystore provider instead of a BouncyCastle provider
findings.body: This method returns KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider(), which is normally a JDK provider such as Sun and can change with the JVM default keystore configuration. That violates the CryptoProvider contract that this method returns the BouncyCastle or BouncyCastle-FIPS provider. Callers using the returned provider for BouncyCastle-specific algorithms, curves, paddings, or keystore types can fail with NoSuchAlgorithmException/NoSuchProviderException or silently use a different implementation than expected. It should return null or an explicit unsupported result, consistent with having no BouncyCastle provider, rather than misidentifying an arbitrary JDK provider.

findings.title: ES384 and ES512 tests reuse a default P-256 key and only test self round-tripping
findings.body: The test constructor generates one EC key pair without specifying a curve, normally P-256, and reuses it for ES256, ES384, and ES512. Consequently the 48-byte ES384 and especially 66-byte ES512 integer paths and DER long-form sequence lengths over 127 bytes produced by real P-521 signatures are not exercised. The assertions also only check that this provider can decode its own encoding; they never verify the generated ASN.1 DER against the original JDK signature or with JDK Signature.verify(). Mutually inverse encoding/decoding errors could therefore pass while producing non-interoperable signatures. Tests should generate P-256, P-384, and P-521 keys respectively and verify interoperability with the JDK signature implementation.

findings.title: No test covers ServiceLoader registration or the new provider-ordering selection
findings.body: The central behavior of this change is that AuthzClientCryptoProvider is discoverable through META-INF/services and that CryptoIntegration chooses the highest-order provider when several providers are present, but the only new test directly constructs AuthzClientCryptoProvider. A broken service registration, an incorrect order value, or a regression in CryptoIntegration sorting would not be caught. A test should load providers through CryptoIntegration/ServiceLoader and assert that the authz provider is selected when alone and that a higher-order provider such as DefaultCryptoProvider wins when both are present.
